title: Diarrhoea
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Feeding and Elimination Problems
Care of Patients with Bowel Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Diarrhoea
headings.content: Diarrhoea is a common clinical condition characterized by an increase in the frequency, fluidity, or volume of bowel movements compared to an individual's normal baseline. In clinical practice, particularly within the context of healthcare in Nigeria and globally, it is formally defined as the passage of three or more loose or liquid stools per day. It is vital for nursing students to differentiate between acute and chronic presentations, as this distinction guides initial assessment and clinical interventions. Acute diarrhoea typically lasts for less than 14 days and is frequently infectious in origin, often linked to contaminated food or water sources. Conversely, chronic diarrhoea persists for longer than four weeks and is usually indicative of underlying non-infectious pathologies, such as inflammatory bowel disease, malabsorption syndromes, or endocrine disorders. Understanding this baseline definition allows nurses to promptly recognize alterations in gastrointestinal function, assess the severity of fluid loss, and initiate appropriate hydration strategies. Furthermore, epidemiological awareness in resource-limited settings emphasizes the importance of recognizing public health threats like cholera or rotavirus, which present with sudden, profuse watery diarrhoea and require immediate public health and clinical responses to prevent high morbidity and mortality among vulnerable populations, especially children under five years of age.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Causes
headings.content: The pathophysiology of diarrhoea involves distinct mechanisms that alter normal intestinal fluid and electrolyte absorption and secretion. These mechanisms are generally categorized into secretory, osmotic, exudative, and motility-related types. Secretory diarrhoea occurs when active ion secretion, often stimulated by bacterial enterotoxins like those from Vibrio cholerae or Escherichia coli, causes large volumes of isotonic fluid to be poured into the intestinal lumen, persisting even during fasting. Osmotic diarrhoea arises when poorly absorbed, osmotically active solutes remain in the bowel lumen, drawing water into the intestine; this type typically resolves when the offending substance, such as lactose or certain antacids, is no longer ingested. Exudative diarrhoea is characterized by the presence of blood, pus, and mucus, resulting from inflammatory or ulcerating conditions of the intestinal mucosa that cause protein and fluid leakage. Motility-related diarrhoea results from rapid transit time through the intestine, reducing the time available for fluid absorption, which can be seen in conditions like irritable bowel syndrome or following gastrointestinal surgeries. Identifying the underlying cause—whether bacterial, viral, parasitic, or dietary—is essential for targeted nursing care, infection control, and medical management in clinical wards.

headings.title: Types and Classification of Diarrhoea
headings.content: Classifying diarrhoea accurately helps healthcare professionals determine the urgency of care and select appropriate interventions. Broadly, diarrhoea is categorized by duration into acute, persistent, and chronic. Acute diarrhoea lasts less than two weeks and is commonly caused by viral agents (such as rotavirus), bacteria (such as Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter), or parasites (such as Giardia lamblia). Persistent diarrhoea lasts between two and four weeks, often transitioning from an acute infection, and carries a high risk of nutritional depletion in children. Chronic diarrhoea lasts longer than four weeks and points toward non-infectious etiologies, including inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, or endocrine disorders like hyperthyroidism. Additionally, clinical classification includes categorizing severity based on dehydration status—no dehydration, some dehydration, or severe dehydration—using standardized assessment tools like the WHO guidelines. Recognizing these types allows nurses in Nigerian hospitals and community clinics to rapidly prioritize patients for fluid resuscitation, nutritional support, and diagnostic workups.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content: The clinical presentation of diarrhoea varies depending on the etiology, duration, and volume of fluid lost. Common symptoms include frequent loose stools, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and malaise. When assessing a patient with diarrhoea, nurses must prioritize evaluating the degree of dehydration. Clinical indicators of dehydration include sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor (skin pinch goes back slowly or very slowly), lethargy or irritability, and a sunken anterior fontanelle in infants. Vital signs often reveal tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension in moderate to severe fluid volume deficits. Furthermore, nurses should inspect the stool characteristics—noting color, consistency, and the presence of blood or mucus, which points toward an invasive bacterial or inflammatory process (dysentery). A thorough nursing assessment also includes reviewing dietary history, recent travel, antibiotic use, and water sources to identify potential epidemiological links, ensuring holistic and safe patient care delivery.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations
headings.content: Diagnostic investigations for diarrhoea are aimed at identifying the underlying cause, assessing electrolyte balance, and ruling out severe systemic complications. Stool analysis is a primary investigation, which includes stool microscopy, culture, and sensitivity to detect bacterial pathogens, ova, and parasites. Stool occult blood testing and fecal leukocyte examinations help differentiate between inflammatory and non-inflammatory causes. In cases of severe or persistent diarrhoea, blood tests are essential; a complete blood count (CBC) may reveal leukocytosis indicating infection or anemia from chronic blood loss, while serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine levels evaluate renal function and electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia or hyponatremia resulting from excessive fluid loss. In specialized settings or for chronic cases, endoscopic procedures, colonoscopy with mucosal biopsies, or breath tests may be ordered. As a nurse, preparing the patient, collecting specimens using aseptic techniques, and monitoring laboratory results promptly are critical responsibilities that ensure timely medical intervention and safe patient outcomes.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of diarrhoea focuses on replacing lost fluids and electrolytes, treating the specific etiology, and reducing symptom severity. Fluid replacement is the cornerstone of therapy, achieved orally using Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) or intravenously in cases of severe dehydration or shock. Zinc supplementation is strongly recommended by the WHO, especially for children under five, as it reduces the duration and severity of diarrheal episodes and prevents future occurrences. Antimicrobial therapy is not routinely prescribed for acute watery diarrhoea because most cases are viral and self-limiting; however, antibiotics are indicated if specific bacterial pathogens are isolated, or if the patient presents with suspected cholera, severe dysentery, or systemic symptoms. Antidiarrheal medications, such as motility inhibitors (e.g., loperamide), are generally avoided in children and in patients with invasive bacterial infections, as they can prolong the illness by trapping pathogens in the gut. Nurses play a crucial role in administering prescribed medications, monitoring the patient's therapeutic response, and educating patients on the rational use of drugs.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Fluid Replacement Therapy
headings.content: Nursing care for a patient with diarrhoea centers around meticulous assessment, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, promoting skin integrity, and providing comfort. The nurse must accurately monitor and record fluid intake and output, including the frequency, volume, and consistency of stools. Weighing the patient daily is a sensitive indicator of fluid balance status. For patients unable to take adequate oral fluids due to severe vomiting or lethargy, initiating and monitoring intravenous fluid therapy (such as normal saline or Ringer's lactate) with precision is a vital nursing skill. Frequent loose stools often cause painful perineal excoriation; therefore, the nurse must implement rigorous skin care by gently cleansing the perianal area after each bowel movement, drying thoroughly, and applying barrier creams. Hand hygiene and standard precautions must be strictly practiced by healthcare staff to prevent the nosocomial spread of infectious agents. Additionally, nurses should monitor for signs of worsening dehydration or electrolyte imbalance and report them promptly to the medical team.

headings.title: Complications and Patient Education
headings.content: Complications of diarrhoea can be life-threatening if not managed promptly, with severe dehydration, hypovolemic shock, electrolyte imbalances (such as hypokalemia leading to cardiac arrhythmias), and acute kidney injury being the most common. Patient education is our strongest tool in preventing recurrence and managing mild episodes at home. Nurses must educate patients and caregivers on proper preparation and administration of Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS), emphasizing that fluids should be given after every loose stool. Education should also cover critical hygiene practices, such as thorough handwashing with soap and water after using the toilet and before handling food, safe drinking water storage, proper food handling, and environmental sanitation. Furthermore, nurses must teach parents and caregivers to recognize danger signs that require immediate return to a healthcare facility, including inability to drink or breastfeed, worsening lethargy, blood in the stool, persistent vomiting, or fever that does not subside. Empowering communities with this knowledge significantly reduces diarrheal morbidity and mortality.
